extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and writers/researchers of crime and detective fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply the genre-defining characteristics of hardboiled (hard-boiled) crime/detective fiction — its protagonists, tone, themes, settings, publication contexts, and relation to noir.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical protagonist — detective who battles organized crime
rubrics_metrics.description: The genre's typical protagonist is a detective who battles the violence of organized crime and deals with a legal system that has become as corrupt as the organized crime itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often portrayed as an antihero rendered cynical by violence; examples given include Dick Tracy, Philip Marlowe, Nick Charles, Mike Hammer, Sam Spade, Lew Archer, Slam Bradley, and The Continental Op. Evaluations or creations should foreground a detective figure confronting criminal/ institutional corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting and historical period — Prohibition-era/urban environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardboiled fiction is closely associated with the period of organized crime that flourished during Prohibition in the United States (1920–1933) and its aftermath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories typically take place in urban settings shaped by gangland violence and corrupt institutions; grounding a work in this milieu (or its modern analogues) aligns it with the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and attitude — tough, cynical, unsentimental
rubrics_metrics.description: Early uses of 'hardboiled' referred to a tough (cynical) attitude towards emotions triggered by violence; protagonists are often rendered cynical by repeated exposure to brutality and corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The voice and perspective should be emotionally guarded, world-weary, and unsentimental rather than sentimental or idealistic; the genre privileges a gritty, hard-edged tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary themes — violence and institutionalized social corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardboiled fiction emphasizes violence and paints a backdrop of institutionalized social corruption rather than focusing primarily on interior psychological states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot and setting should foreground systemic corruption (e.g., corrupt legal system, organized crime) and physical danger/violence as central forces shaping characters and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and form — pulp magazines and paperback originals
rubrics_metrics.description: From its earliest days, hardboiled fiction was published in and closely associated with pulp magazines (most famously Black Mask) and later with paperback-original houses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the pulp magazine and paperback-original formats helps explain stylistic and pacing expectations (concise, plot-driven, serialized installments); citing or emulating pulp venues and formats is appropriate for authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to noir fiction — external social focus vs interior focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardboiled writing is associated with noir fiction but differs in emphasis: noir's primary focus is interior (psychic imbalance, self-hatred, sociopathy), whereas hardboiled 'paints a backdrop of institutionalized social corruption.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When distinguishing or blending genres, emphasize whether the work foregrounds external social/institutional corruption (hardboiled) or the character's internal psychological collapse (noir); this distinction affects tone, character motivation, and thematic emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stock elements and characters — femmes fatales and similar tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Femmes fatales were standard fare in hardboiled fiction, alongside other recurring stock characters and tropes drawn from crime and detective traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of archetypal figures (femme fatale, corrupt officials, gangsters, world-weary detectives) is typical; such elements should serve the genre’s moral ambiguity and thematic focus on corruption and survival rather than melodramatic cliché.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre distinction — private-eye story vs crime novel
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulp/hardboiled fiction is often used synonymously with crime or gangster fiction, but some distinguish the private-eye story (focused on a detective protagonist) from the broader crime novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When categorizing or crafting work, clarify whether the piece centers on a private-eye perspective (investigation-driven, first-person or close third) or on other crime-novel forms (broader ensemble, procedural, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic lineage and exemplars — learn from pioneers
rubrics_metrics.description: The style was pioneered and popularized by writers such as Carroll John Daly, Dashiell Hammett, James M. Cain, and Raymond Chandler, with an influential heyday in 1930s–50s America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study canonical works by these authors to internalize genre conventions (voice, moral ambiguity, plotting, depiction of corruption); later practitioners and paperback publishers (Gold Medal, Black Lizard) continued the tradition and can serve as models.
